title: The Device's Own Clock: Ticks That Wrap and Drift

questions.question: A device stamps messages in milliseconds on sixteen bits. Two stamps 10 ms apart are 65531 and 5. What does a subtraction written as an int give?
options: -65526, because the unsigned values are promoted to int before the subtraction
questions.explanation: The difference has to be taken in the counter's own width, so it wraps the way the counter does. Taken in int it is a duration of minus a minute.

questions.question: Using the first message's clock offset for ever was 185 ms wrong after an hour. Why does it grow?
options: The device's oscillator runs a little fast or slow, 50 ppm here, so the offset between the two clocks changes steadily
questions.explanation: 50 parts per million over 3600 seconds is 180 ms. An offset is a measurement of one instant, not a constant.

questions.question: Why does ClockMap keep the least delayed sample in each bucket rather than the average?
options: An arrival time is the send time plus a delay that is never negative, so the least delayed sample is the closest to the truth and the line must lie under the rest
Averages are not defined for times
questions.explanation: Jitter only adds. Averaging would put the delay into the estimate, and the minimum finds the floor.

questions.question: The map's error was measured against the send time plus 2 ms. Why not the send time itself?
options: The least delay cannot be separated from the clock offset without a second clock, so it is the part nobody on one side of the link can know
questions.explanation: For fusing two sensors that share the host the constant cancels. For absolute time it does not, and the lesson names it instead of hiding it.

questions.question: A device resets and the map is not told. Why is every timestamp wrong by the time the device was off, for ten minutes?
options: The unwrapped timeline carries on without the downtime, so every old bucket is that far out, and the fit averages them with the new ones until they leave the window
questions.explanation: Measured, 5011 ms for a five second reset, and 3.5 ms when the map was reset on the restart.

questions.question: How does the unwrapper tell a device reset from a message that arrived late?
options: A link delivers in order, so a stamp that goes backwards is a reset; and a silence of more than half a turn looks like one, which is the counter's limit
questions.explanation: A counter can see a gap just under half its range. Past that, a gap and a restart cannot be told apart, which is why a boot counter in the message is the better design.
